blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A pole is 40 years old in 2027, the plan's first year. A repair that leaves it with half its age starts in 2028 and takes one year. Under the lesson's convention, how old is the pole in 2030?

options.text: 22, since it is half of 42 in 2029 and has aged one more year since then
options.says: Right: the work ends in 2028, so from 2029 the pole is 0.5 x (40 + 2) = 21, and 22 in 2030.

options.text: 21.5, since it is half of 41, its age when the work began, plus one more year
options.says: The pole keeps aging during the work; the share applies to the age it has reached when the work ends, 42.

options.text: 43, since the repair changes the risk coefficient and leaves the age as it was
options.says: The work changes the age itself; every risk number follows from the new age.

options.text: 21, since it is half of 42 in 2029 and keeps that age from then on
options.says: After the work the asset ages again, one year per year.

origin.section: Work Resets the Asset's Age in the Year After It Ends

questions.stem: A plan covers 2027 to 2031. A two-year replacement may start in 2027, 2028, 2029 or 2030, and its coefficient counts only the risk removed inside the plan's years. What does the solver see for the 2030 start?

options.text: The largest coefficient, since a later start replaces an older and riskier asset
options.says: Each in-service year removes a little more, but the 2030 start has no in-service year inside the plan.

options.text: The same coefficient as the 2027 start, since each start removes equal risk
options.says: Later starts are in service for fewer counted years; P024's plan-years column falls from 546 to 0.

options.text: A coefficient of zero, since the asset is first in service in 2032, after the plan
options.says: Right: that is the end-of-horizon effect; a fixed evaluation window fixes it.

options.text: A negative coefficient, since the years of work add risk that the plan must carry
options.says: During the work the asset keeps its old risk, so the reduction is 0, not negative.

origin.section: Count the Reduction Over a Fixed Window and Discount It

questions.stem: A team has the NPV start-year model of lesson 6.4.2 and now wants the plan that removes the most failure risk within the same rules. What change to the model does that take?

options.text: New rows capping each year's risk, keeping the objective as it is
options.says: A cap limits risk but still maximizes NPV; the most risk removed needs the risk coefficients in the objective.

options.text: New rr coefficients in the objective, keeping the rows as they are
options.says: Right: rr[i,t] replaces npv[i,t] in the objective; sets, variables and rows stay.

options.text: New age variables for each asset, keeping the rows as they are
options.says: Each start year fixes the whole age path, so the ages are computed before the solve and need no variables.

options.text: New piecewise rows for the risk curve, keeping the objective as it is
options.says: The curve is evaluated ahead of time for each start year, so the model stays linear with no piecewise rows.

origin.section: The Coefficients Enter the Start-Year Model Unchanged
